forces.title: Elevated UK Industrial Energy Costs Undermine Competitiveness
forces.description: UK industrial electricity and gas prices are approximately 75% higher than the G7 average, severely challenging the competitiveness of energy-intensive industries such as steel. These elevated costs inflate operating expenses, diminish investment returns, and weaken the business case for expanding domestic production. This situation risks slowing reindustrialization efforts, undermining supply chain resilience, and making the UK less attractive for industrial investment, potentially increasing reliance on imported goods.

forces.title: Global Steel Overcapacity Compresses Industry Margins
forces.description: The global steel industry suffers from persistent overcapacity, with a production capacity exceeding 2.5 billion tons in 2024 against a demand of only about 1.9 billion tons. Much of this surplus capacity originates from China, which rapidly expanded manufacturing to support its urbanization and industrialization. This imbalance significantly compresses margins for steel producers worldwide, making cost control and regional competitiveness increasingly critical in a fragmented market shaped by policy and resource constraints.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: High European Energy Costs Burden Green Steel Transition
forces.description: European Direct Reduced Iron-Electric Arc Furnace (DRI-EAF) steel production faces a significant cost disadvantage due to high natural gas prices. For example, Sweden's gas prices are 4-5 times higher than Oman's, adding approximately $250/ton to steel costs. Germany's electricity costs are also nearly double Oman's. These disparities make European DRI-EAF costs 45-50% higher than in competitive regions, severely constraining the business case for low-carbon steel investments and increasing reliance on policy support or green premiums.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: DRI-EAF Long-Term Competitiveness Threatened by Input Scarcity
forces.description: While Direct Reduced Iron-Electric Arc Furnace (DRI-EAF) technology offers a crucial pathway to lower-emissions steel, its long-term competitiveness faces significant constraints. These include intensifying competition for natural gas, a primary input for the DRI process, and limited availability of high-quality prime scrap. These factors can increase input costs and operational challenges, potentially hindering the scalability and economic viability of green steel production, especially in regions without abundant, low-cost natural gas or ample domestic scrap resources.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Iron Ore Project Delays Impact Upstream Supply Reliability
forces.description: Major high-grade iron ore projects, crucial inputs for steelmaking, frequently experience significant delays, impacting upstream supply reliability. For instance, Guinea's Simandou project, the world's largest untapped high-grade ore deposit, took three decades to move from exploration to production by 2025. These extensive delays are often attributable to political changes and persistent financing hurdles, creating uncertainty and potential cost increases for steel producers reliant on secure and timely access to raw materials.
forces.source_title: African bedrock: How the continent’s minerals can help power the world

forces.title: Global Metal Price Volatility Threatens Steel Industry Margins
forces.description: The metals market has entered an era defined by extreme price volatility, with average annual price swings for key metals surging by 22 percentage points between 2021 and 2025 compared to the prior five-year period. This includes critical steel inputs like nickel. Such significant and persistent volatility threatens the traditional business model of metals and mining companies, including steel producers, by eroding profit margins and destabilizing cash flows, demanding proactive commercial excellence and risk management strategies to mitigate downside risks.
forces.source_title: From Volume to Value: The $20 Billion Commercial Payoff in Metals and Mining

forces.title: Post-Stockpiling Demand Correction Risks Price Falls
forces.description: The recent surge in metals prices, including 40-50% for some steel products, has been partly driven by stockpiling motivated by tariffs, quotas, and geopolitical events since February 2026. While these protective measures offer short-term support, this front-loaded demand creates a significant risk. There is a strong possibility that demand and prices could correct downwards once buying patterns normalize and stockpiles are consumed, leading to potential market instability and financial pressure on the steel sector.

forces.title: Green Steel Transition Reshaping European Production Landscape
forces.description: Europe's steel industry is undergoing a fundamental structural transformation, moving away from traditional Blast Furnace-Basic Oxygen Furnace (BF-BOF) technology towards more environmentally friendly Electric Arc Furnace (EAF) and Direct Reduced Iron-EAF (DRI-EAF) routes. This shift is driven by stringent environmental regulations, carbon pricing mechanisms like the EU ETS, and increasing sustainability considerations. New investments, exemplified by projects like Salzgitter's Salcos facility in Germany, are predominantly targeting DRI-EAF plants with smaller carbon footprints, gradually phasing out older, higher-emission capacity.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Geopolitical Shifts Drive Supply Chain Reorganization in Materials
forces.description: Rising geopolitical tensions, increased trade fragmentation, and localized disruptions are fundamentally reshaping material supply chains, including those for steel. This necessitates a shift from models optimized primarily for cost and efficiency to those prioritizing resilience and security of supply. The reorganization includes significant reshoring of industrial processes, causing a step change in domestic materials demand. This structural force impacts lead times, inventory strategies, and the overall reliability expectations for material wholesalers and service centers.
forces.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

forces.title: Divergent Investment Archetypes Emerge in Global Steel
forces.description: The global steel industry is experiencing a fundamental shift in investment strategies, leading to three distinct archetypes. Cost-driven investment remains centered on high-CO2 BF-BOF technology in India and China. Transition-positioned investment favors DRI-EAF in regions with favorable gas economics like the Middle East and the United States, operating without significant subsidies. Policy-dependent investment in DRI-EAF or hydrogen-powered DRI-EAF is concentrated in Europe, viable only with rising carbon prices, phased-out allowances, or substantial green premium and subsidy support.
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: Increasing Market Liquidity Fuels Price Volatility
forces.description: The metals market is becoming increasingly liquid, with trading volumes on exchanges such as the Shanghai Futures Exchange now rivaling the London Metal Exchange. This enhanced liquidity contributes significantly to price volatility by making market prices more responsive to short-term supply and demand dynamics, as well as broader macroeconomic and geopolitical events. While offering opportunities for market participants, this cyclical change necessitates greater agility and sophisticated risk management strategies for steel producers to navigate rapidly shifting price landscapes.
forces.source_title: From Volume to Value: The $20 Billion Commercial Payoff in Metals and Mining

forces.title: Decarbonization Drives Demand for Lower-Emissions Steel
forces.description: Decarbonization goals and sustainability considerations are increasingly driving demand for lower-emissions steel. Technologies such as Direct Reduced Iron-Electric Arc Furnace (DRI-EAF) significantly reduce CO2 emissions compared to traditional methods and are gaining importance as carbon pricing increases. This creates an upside opportunity for steelmakers adopting greener production routes, especially in regions with supportive policies like the EU ETS and Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which favor low-emissions products and enable a 'green premium.'
forces.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

forces.title: New Technologies & Reshoring Accelerate Materials Demand
forces.description: New demand engines, including artificial intelligence (AI), electric vehicles (EVs), and renewable-energy infrastructure, are generating sustained high demand for critical materials like steel. Concurrently, geopolitical realignments are driving reshoring of many industrial processes, causing a significant step change in domestic materials demand in regions like North America and Europe. This combination is expected to accelerate materials consumption, which was stagnant between 2015 and 2024, leading to sustained growth for steel and related components through 2030.
forces.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

forces.title: Defence Spending Boosts Demand for Industrial Materials
forces.description: European countries are significantly increasing defense spending, with projected outlays of €700-€800 billion for 2022-2028. This modernization and ammunition replenishment drive is fueling an 18% annual growth in relevant materials categories, which directly impacts the demand for industrial materials, including steel. The shift towards 'just-in-case' industrial models for stockpiles and supply chain depth also emphasizes the strategic importance of domestic material production and resilience, creating a sustained demand for related manufacturing.
forces.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

viewpoints.title: UK Metals Sector Sees Price Gains, Remains Financially Fragile
viewpoints.description: The UK metals sector, including steel, is experiencing improved pricing and short-term trading conditions, with some steel products seeing 40-50% price increases since February 2026. This uplift is driven by tariffs, quotas, and geopolitical events prompting stockpiling, with protective measures expected to sustain conditions through the latter half of the year. However, the sector remains financially fragile and Europe lags other regions, while rising logistics, raw material, and energy costs exacerbate financing and working-capital requirements. There's a risk of demand and price correction once stockpiling normalizes.

viewpoints.title: Global Steel Demand Set for Sustained Growth to 2030
viewpoints.description: After a period of marginal change from 2015 to 2024, global consumption of steel, aluminum, copper, and stainless steel is projected to accelerate, returning to sustained growth by 2030. This resurgence is fueled by new demand engines, including artificial intelligence, electric vehicles, and renewable-energy infrastructure, alongside geopolitical realignment leading to reshoring of industrial processes. This structural shift is expected to increase domestic materials demand significantly, indicating a positive outlook for the steel sector's growth trajectory.
viewpoints.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

viewpoints.title: Asian BF-BOF Steel More Cost-Competitive Than European Green Steel
viewpoints.description: Steel production using Blast Furnace-Basic Oxygen Furnace (BF-BOF) technology in India and China is currently the most cost-competitive globally, significantly undercutting Direct Reduced Iron-Electric Arc Furnace (DRI-EAF) methods in other regions. For instance, Indian BF-BOF steel is $120/ton cheaper than Oman's DRI-EAF. This is primarily due to access to low-cost coal and strong domestic demand. Conversely, European green steel investments, despite policy support, face substantially higher natural gas and electricity costs, making them 45-50% more expensive than competitors like Oman for DRI-EAF production.
viewpoints.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

demand_drivers.description: Rapid urbanization and industrialization in countries like China previously drove massive capacity expansion, leading to current global oversupply in steel.

pnl_drivers.description: Global excess capacity in steel production significantly compresses margins for steel producers, reflecting a fundamental supply-demand imbalance in the industry.

market_sizing.methodology: Global crude steel industry capacity was over 2.5 billion tons in 2024, compared to demand of approximately 1.9 billion tons. This indicates a significant global overcapacity in the steel sector, primarily driven by China's past rapid urbanization and industrialization.
market_sizing.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

demand_drivers.description: Demand for lower-emissions steel is driven by increasingly stringent environmental regulations (e.g., EU ETS), rising carbon pricing, and growing public opinion supporting industrial decarbonization efforts.

new_opportunities.description: The transition to low-carbon steel production offers the opportunity to capture a 'green premium' as carbon pricing increases and free allowances for traditional methods are phased out, creating an economic surplus.

market_sizing.methodology: Plans are underway in Europe for more than 17 Electric Arc Furnace (EAF) and Direct Reduced Iron-EAF steel plants to produce roughly 40 to 50 million tons of low-carbon steel by 2030. This represents a significant projected shift towards environmentally friendlier steel production methods within the region.
market_sizing.source_title: EAF steel: Beyond the blast furnace

pnl_drivers.description: Improved commercial strategies, including hedging, shifting portfolios, and holding inventory, protect profit margins and capitalize on heightened market volatility, which averaged 22 percentage points higher between 2021-2025.

new_opportunities.description: Exploiting the increased liquidity and financialization of metals markets to generate significant value beyond core production activities, through sophisticated trading and risk management.

market_sizing.methodology: Metals and mining companies can unlock a potential $20 billion annual value pool by evolving from traditional production-centric models to becoming market players engaged in commercial and trading activities. This is achieved through active management of sales, marketing, optimization, and trading levers, capitalizing on market volatility and protecting profit margins.
market_sizing.source_title: From Volume to Value: The $20 Billion Commercial Payoff in Metals and Mining

demand_drivers.description: High-grade iron ore, like that from Simandou, is a critical input for efficient steelmaking, offering the potential to reduce CO2 emissions from ironmaking by 5% per metric ton compared to lower-grade ores.

market_sizing.methodology: The Simandou project in Guinea, recognized as the world's largest untapped reserve of high-grade iron ore, is projected to deliver 120 million metric tons of iron ore per year at full production, having moved from exploration to production in 2025.
market_sizing.source_title: African bedrock: How the continent’s minerals can help power the world

demand_drivers.description: Corporate climate commitments and environmental regulations are increasingly driving demand for materials with lower carbon footprints, including green steel, to meet sustainability targets.

pnl_drivers.description: Producers of green metals may achieve higher margins or enhanced market access due to differentiated product offerings and capabilities such as carbon reporting and recycling integration, driven by buyer preferences.

market_sizing.methodology: Globally, buyers anticipate increasing the share of green metals in their procurement from approximately 21% today to 32% by 2030. This indicates a significant shift in material specifications driven by decarbonization and sustainability objectives, impacting demand for conventionally produced metals.
market_sizing.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain
